name: CLI Argument Parsing (argparse)
description: solution_code (Python) defines a single top-level function `build_parser()` (no arguments) that constructs and returns a real, fully-configured `argparse.ArgumentParser` instance implementing the CLI interface described in task_description -- flags, options, required/optional args, type coercion, choices, mutually-exclusive groups, and/or subcommands via add_subparsers(). The harness calls build_parser() EXACTLY ONCE, then drives the SAME parser instance through every one of invocations' own ordered argv lists via real, unmodified `parser.parse_args(argv)` calls (confirmed empirically safe -- CPython's argparse has copied action='append'/'extend' default lists per call since 3.8, so no cross-invocation state leaks through the shared instance for any standard action). Each invocation declares its own required outcome: EITHER a successful parse (expected_namespace, matched via exact-value equality against parse_args' own real returned Namespace.__dict__) OR a real parse failure (argparse's own convention: a validation error inside parse_args always raises SystemExit via self.error(), never a catchable exception -- expected_exit_code plus an expected_error_substring that must literally appear in the real captured stderr text, chosen deliberately over exact stderr matching since argparse's own message wording is verbose/formatting-sensitive but its VALIDATION-KIND vocabulary -- 'required', 'invalid choice', 'invalid int value', 'not allowed with argument', 'unrecognized arguments' -- is stable stdlib convention, empirically confirmed against a live Python 3 argparse rather than assumed). There is no independent oracle re-deriving what a CORRECT parser for this row's own natural-language task_description should be (task_description is open-ended prose, exactly the kind of thing this registry already trusts curator-authored ground truth for elsewhere -- numerical_precision's expected_output, retry_backoff_resilience's expected_result -- rather than mechanically re-deriving); invocations' own expected_namespace/expected_exit_code/expected_error_substring are curator-authored claims, checked directly against solution_code's own REAL argparse execution, mitigated by this pipeline's own llm + human_audit stages downstream of execution, the same trust model and residual already accepted for those two sibling categories.
executionEnv: python3 (stdlib argparse/contextlib/io/json only -- zero new sandbox dependencies; click/yargs are deliberately out of scope for this category, a prior scoping decision preserved here).

fields.label: Task description
fields.help: Natural-language description of a realistic CLI tool's argument interface, precise enough that a contributor reading only this field can implement build_parser() correctly -- e.g. 'a file-conversion tool taking --input/-i (required, path string), --output/-o (optional, defaults to None meaning stdout), --format (choices: json/yaml/csv, required), and a --verbose/-v flag (store_true, default False)'; 'a backup tool with subcommands `create` and `restore` (use add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)) -- create takes --source (required string) and --compress (store_true flag); restore takes --archive (required string) and --target (optional string, default None)'; 'a rate-limiter config tool with a REQUIRED mutually-exclusive group (add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)) holding --requests-per-second and --requests-per-minute, each type=int and exactly one must be supplied, and its value must be a positive integer (use a custom type= callable raising argparse.ArgumentTypeError for a non-positive value, never a bare type=int alone, if the row's own invocations exercise the positive-integer constraint specifically)'. State every flag's exact name(s), whether it is required, its type coercion (str is argparse's own default; state explicitly when it must be int/float/a custom validated type), its default value when optional, and its choices/constraints -- this is the sole natural-language contract a contributor implements against; invocations below is the sole mechanically-checked ground truth, authored independently by the curator applying THIS description's own rules by hand against a real argparse run, never inferred from solution_code.

fields.label: Parser builder (Python)
fields.help: THE GRADED ARTIFACT. Python code defining EXACTLY ONE top-level function named `build_parser`, with EXACTLY this signature: `def build_parser():` -- no arguments; it must construct and `return` a real `argparse.ArgumentParser` instance (or an instance of a subclass of it) configured per task_description, using argparse's own real, standard machinery: add_argument() for individual flags/options/positionals, add_mutually_exclusive_group() for mutually-exclusive flag sets, add_subparsers() plus each subparser's own add_parser()/add_argument() calls for a subcommand-based interface. MECHANICALLY ENFORCED, NOT OPTIONAL: the harness calls build_parser() and checks `isinstance(returned_value, argparse.ArgumentParser)` before running a single invocation -- returning anything else (a hand-rolled dict/if-elif dispatcher, a dataclass, a plain object impersonating a few methods) is a real, immediate structural rejection, not something later invocation checks might happen to still catch; this already rules out the overwhelming majority of a 'fake parser' attack on its own, since genuinely reimplementing the full ArgumentParser interface convincingly (parse_args' own signature, error/usage formatting, subparsers, mutually-exclusive-group enforcement, type-coercion exception handling) is far more work than just using the real stdlib class. CALLING CONVENTION: build_parser() is called EXACTLY ONCE per row; the SAME returned parser instance is then reused for every one of invocations' own `parser.parse_args(argv)` calls, in the invocations array's own declared order -- never rebuilt between invocations. This mirrors how a real long-running test harness (or REPL-style tool) would exercise one parser instance repeatedly, and is confirmed empirically safe against CPython's real argparse (no cross-invocation state leak through a shared action='append'/'extend' default list, fixed in CPython since Python 3.8) -- solution_code does not need to guard against this, but must not itself introduce cross-call state (e.g. a global counter mutated by a custom type= callable) that would make two identical argv lists parse differently on a second call, since nothing about this category's own contract expects or permits that. solution_code must NEVER call `parser.parse_args()` itself, never read sys.argv, and never call sys.exit()/print() at module scope -- it only builds and returns the configured parser; the harness owns every parse_args() call and its own argv.

fields.label: Invocation sequence
fields.help: JSON array of 4-20 invocations, each independently run against the SAME parser instance (see solution_code's own help text on the calling convention) in the given order, each one of two shapes distinguished by its own required `outcome` key: SUCCESS -- `{"argv": [<strings>], "outcome": "success", "expected_namespace": {<plain-identifier key>: <JSON string|number|boolean|null, or a flat array of such scalars>, ...}}` -- expected_namespace must equal, via EXACT value equality (order-independent for keys, order-SIGNIFICANT for any array value), the real `vars(parser.parse_args(argv))` dict solution_code's own parser produces -- author it by hand-tracing task_description's own rules (every declared dest, including every default value for an arg NOT supplied in this particular argv, and -- for a subcommand interface -- ONLY the dest keys that specific subcommand's own subparser actually defines, since a different subcommand invocation legitimately has a different key set). FAILURE -- `{"argv": [<strings>], "outcome": "failure", "expected_exit_code": <int 1-255>, "expected_error_substring": <string, 3-200 chars>}` -- argparse's own convention: any real validation failure inside parse_args() calls self.error(), which prints a usage+message line to STDERR and unconditionally calls sys.exit(2) (2 is virtually always the correct expected_exit_code for stdlib ArgumentParser; empirically confirmed against a live Python 3 run for every failure kind below) -- the harness wraps parse_args() in a real try/except SystemExit, checks the exception's own real .code against expected_exit_code, and checks expected_error_substring is a literal substring of the real captured stderr text (contextlib.redirect_stderr around the call; never exact stderr matching, since argparse's own usage-line wording is verbose and formatting-sensitive, but its validation-KIND vocabulary is stable stdlib convention) -- author expected_error_substring using argparse's own EMPIRICALLY-CONFIRMED stable phrases for the failure kind being tested, never guessed: a missing required argument (or an unfilled required mutually-exclusive group) always includes the word 'required' (e.g. 'the following arguments are required: --input/-i', 'one of the arguments --requests-per-second --requests-per-minute is required'); an out-of-choices value always includes 'invalid choice' (e.g. "invalid choice: 'xml'"); a `type=int` coercion failure always includes 'invalid int value'; a violated mutually-exclusive group always includes 'not allowed with argument'; an extra/unknown token always includes 'unrecognized arguments'. A row testing a CUSTOM type= callable's own raised argparse.ArgumentTypeError message (e.g. a positive-integer validator) should use THAT callable's own exact message text as the substring instead, since argparse embeds it verbatim rather than wrapping it in one of the generic phrases above. ANTI-HARDCODING, MECHANICALLY ENFORCED (dataset-authoring-defect gates, checked before solution_code is ever run): (1) at least 4 invocations total -- a handful of invocations is the minimum needed to exercise more than one code path; (2) at least 2 invocations must be outcome "success" with MUTUALLY DIFFERENT expected_namespace values -- a parser that only ever needs to get ONE specific argv combination right cannot be meaningfully distinguished from one that coincidentally, degenerately matches it; (3) at least 1 invocation must be outcome "failure" -- a row that never exercises real validation-failure behavior cannot prove solution_code implements required/choices/type constraints correctly, only that it accepts good input. AUTHORING GUIDANCE: cover the REAL shape declared in task_description -- for a subcommand interface, include invocations for every subcommand plus at least one subcommand-selection failure (an invalid/missing subcommand name); for a mutually-exclusive group, include one invocation violating it (both supplied) and, if the group is required, one omitting it entirely; for a type=int/custom-type field, include one invocation with a non-coercible value.
